passage: The science exhibition was the next morning, and the power had just gone out in the school lab. By the light of her phone torch, Baljeet held up her water-filter model for Kiran ma'am. "The sand layer is in the wrong order," ma'am said flatly. "And your chart claims it makes water safe to drink. You haven't tested that. A judge will catch it in ten seconds." Baljeet's face went hot. She'd spent three weekends on it. "You could have said something nice first," she muttered, jaw tight. Kiran ma'am didn't flinch. "I'm saying this because you're capable of first prize. Come, we'll fix the layers together before the lights come back." Baljeet stood stiffly for a moment, then picked up the gravel.

qa.q: What was wrong with the sand layer?
qa.a: The sand layer was in the wrong order.

qa.q: Why did Baljeet mutter "You could have said something nice first"?
qa.a: She felt stung and angry after three weekends of work, and the flat words hurt more because they came the night before the exhibition.

qa.q: What turning point is available to Baljeet in this moment?
qa.a: Picking up the gravel and fixing the layers with Kiran ma'am turns the sting into improvement, letting her see the critique as help from someone who believes in her.

qa.q: How might Kiran ma'am feel when Baljeet mutters at her?
qa.a: She may feel a flicker of discomfort but stays steady, because she cares more about Baljeet doing her best than about being liked in that moment.

grounding: Under time pressure a teacher bluntly critiques a teenage girl's project; she feels stung and angry, then accepts the warm, high-standard help.

passage: Vidya had edited her short film until two a.m., and now it played on the classroom projector in their Bengaluru school. When the lights came on, Pranav sir leaned back. "The shots are lovely. The story isn't there yet. Your ending tells me what to feel instead of showing me. And the middle drags by a full minute." A couple of classmates shifted in their seats. Vidya stared at her notebook, cheeks burning. Who asked him? she thought, and then, unfairly, that he'd never liked her work. After class he stopped by her desk. "I wouldn't bother if I didn't think it could be great. Cut the minute and show me the ending. I'll watch it again Friday." Vidya nodded without looking up, but she opened her laptop on the bus home.

qa.q: How long did Pranav sir say the middle dragged?
qa.a: The middle drags by a full minute.

qa.q: What was Vidya thinking when the lights came on and her cheeks burned?
qa.a: She was stung and briefly angry, thinking "Who asked him?" and unfairly deciding he'd never liked her work.

qa.q: What did Pranav sir do that turned harsh feedback into mentoring?
qa.a: He followed the blunt critique with warmth after class, saying he believed the film could be great and offering to watch it again on Friday.

qa.q: What might Pranav sir experience as Vidya nods without looking up?
qa.a: He may be unsure how his words landed and hope she can see past the sting, trusting that his high standards come from care.

grounding: A teacher gives a teenage girl blunt feedback on her film; she feels stung and angry, but his warm follow-up shows the critique as care.

passage:
The school science fair was two weeks away, and Pema brought her water-filter model to the lab at lunch. Sharmila ma'am looked at it for a long time.
"The design is neat. The test is weak. You tested it once, with tap water, and called it a success."
Pema's face went hot. She had spent four evenings on it. "It works, ma'am."
"Once. I want to see it work five times, with muddy water, and I want the numbers."
Pema grabbed the model and left without a word. In the corridor she kicked the bin, then stood still.
That evening she filled five jars with muddy water.

qa.q: How many evenings had Pema spent on the model?
qa.a: Four evenings.

qa.q: What was Pema feeling when she grabbed the model and left?
qa.a: She felt stung and angry after working hard, feeling the blunt comments were unfair to her effort.

qa.q: What turning point is available to Pema at this stage?
qa.a: Using the criticism as a to-do list, as she starts to by filling five jars, and going back to show the results.

qa.q: How might Sharmila ma'am feel as Pema walks out without a word?
qa.a: She may feel uneasy, hoping the high bar will help Pema rather than push her away.

grounding: Shows a student stung and briefly angry at her teacher's blunt critique, then starting to use it.

passage:
Dear Karthik sir,
I'm writing because I walked out of the lab angry on Friday, and I wanted to explain.
When you said my robotics project "looks good but doesn't solve anything," I felt like my face was burning. I went home and told my mother you didn't understand it. She just said, "Beti, sleep on it." I didn't sleep well.
On Sunday I read your comments again. You were right that the arm only picks up objects of one size. You also wrote "You can fix this. I've seen you fix harder things." I hadn't noticed that line on Friday.
I've started a new gripper design. Could I show you on Wednesday?
Sangeeta

qa.q: What did Karthik sir say about the robotics project?
qa.a: That it "looks good but doesn't solve anything".

qa.q: What was Sangeeta feeling on Friday when she walked out?
qa.a: She felt angry and stung, her face burning, and at first believed sir did not understand her project.

qa.q: What small step shows Sangeeta using the critique well?
qa.a: Rereading the comments calmly on Sunday and starting a new gripper design to show on Wednesday.

qa.q: What might Karthik sir feel when he reads this email?
qa.a: He may feel relieved and glad that his blunt words, backed by his encouraging line, reached her.

grounding: Shows a student stung and angry at her mentor's blunt critique who later sees the care in it.

passage:
Okay, so you want the honest version? Fine. Bidisha ma'am read the first chapter of my short story in front of me and said, "The opening is lazy. You're better than this." Just like that.
I was so angry I didn't talk to her for two days. I told my friends she hated me. But then I noticed she had written notes on every page, in green pen, tiny handwriting. Nobody writes that much for someone they hate, you know?
So I rewrote the opening. Three times. The third one she read and just smiled.
That's when it clicked for me, Mahima, the girl who used to hide her stories in a drawer. The hard feedback was her caring.

qa.q: What colour pen did Bidisha ma'am use for her notes?
qa.a: Green.

qa.q: How did Mahima feel after Bidisha ma'am called the opening lazy?
qa.a: Mahima felt so angry and stung that she stopped talking to her for two days and believed ma'am hated her.

qa.q: What turning point helped Mahima move past the hurt?
qa.a: Noticing the notes on every page, which showed care, and then rewriting the opening three times.

qa.q: What might Bidisha ma'am have felt during the two days of silence?
qa.a: She may have felt uneasy or sad at the distance, while trusting Mahima would come back to the work.

grounding: Shows a student stung and angry at her teacher's blunt critique who later sees the high standard as care.

passage:
Tuesday. Rukmini Ma'am handed back Uma's project on river pollution with red ink all over the second half. "Your data is strong, but your conclusion ignores half of it. You can do much better than this." Uma's face burned. She had stayed up till midnight. She stuffed the file into her bag without a word.
Wednesday. Uma told her friend, "She hates me now." Then she reread the comments at night. Annoyingly, they were right. At the bottom, in small letters, Ma'am had written: "I push because you can go far."
The following Monday. Uma brought a new draft. Rukmini Ma'am read it slowly, then smiled. "Now this is your real work." Uma walked out feeling taller, and slightly embarrassed about Wednesday.

qa.q: What was Uma's project about?
qa.a: Her project was on river pollution.

qa.q: What was Uma feeling when she stuffed the file into her bag?
qa.a: She felt stung and angry, her face burning after staying up till midnight on it.

qa.q: What helped Uma turn the criticism into better work?
qa.a: Rereading the comments calmly and seeing they were right, helped by the note showing the teacher pushed her because she could go far.

qa.q: What might Rukmini Ma'am be feeling as she writes the red comments?
qa.a: She probably cares and has high hopes for Uma, even knowing the bluntness will sting, as her note 'you can go far' shows.

grounding: Shows a teacher bluntly critiquing a student's project with warmth underneath, and the student moving from stung anger to seeing the criticism as a gift.
